overview:
Bahrain is a small island country in the Persian Gulf, which Arab nations call the Arabian Gulf, tucked between Saudi Arabia and the Qatar peninsula. It is made up of one main island and about 30 smaller ones, covering roughly 765 km², about the size of New York City. A 25-kilometer causeway links it to Saudi Arabia by road.

Around 1.5 million people live in Bahrain, and more than half of them are workers from other countries, especially India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines. Most live in and around the capital, Manama, a modern city of glass towers, shopping malls and an old market called the souq. Arabic is the official language, and English is widely used in business.

Bahrain is a kingdom ruled by the Al Khalifa family since 1783, with a partly elected parliament. For thousands of years it grew rich from pearls fished from its shallow waters; today oil, banking and aluminum are the main industries, and it hosts the Middle East's first Formula 1 race.
landAndNature:
Bahrain is low, flat and dry. Its highest point, Jabal ad Dukhan or Mountain of Smoke, is only about 134 meters high. Most of the land is limestone desert, but freshwater springs once bubbled up from underground, even beneath the sea, which is why the name Bahrain means "two seas" in Arabic. Those springs watered date palm groves along the northern coast.

Summers are scorching and humid, often above 40 degrees Celsius, while winters are mild. Land has been reclaimed from the sea to build new neighborhoods. Offshore, the Hawar Islands are home to a huge colony of Socotra cormorants and to dugongs, gentle sea mammals that graze on seagrass. In the middle of the desert stands the Tree of Life, a lone mesquite tree about 400 years old with no obvious water source.
peopleAndCulture:
Bahrainis are Arabs, most of them Muslim, and Arabic is the language of daily life alongside English, Hindi, Urdu and Tagalog spoken by foreign workers. The national dish, machboos, is spiced rice with chicken, lamb or fish; sweet, gooey halwa flavored with saffron and rosewater is a favorite treat, and strong Arabic coffee is offered to every guest.

The pearl-diving past lives on in fidjeri songs, which crews of divers once sang on their boats. Falconry, camel racing and horse racing are traditional pastimes, while soccer is the most popular modern sport. The Bahrain Grand Prix has drawn Formula 1 fans since 2004. Ramadan is a time of evening feasts, and Eid holidays fill the streets with families and sweets.
history:
About 4,000 years ago Bahrain was the center of Dilmun, a trading civilization that linked Mesopotamia to the Indus Valley; tens of thousands of its burial mounds still dot the island. Persians, Greeks and Arab tribes ruled in turn, and Islam arrived in the 600s. Pearls from Bahrain were prized across the ancient world.

The Portuguese seized the island in 1521 and built a fort that still stands; Persian rulers followed, and in 1783 the Al Khalifa family took control. From 1861 Bahrain was a British protectorate, and in 1932 it became the first country on the Arab side of the Gulf to strike oil. Independence came in 1971. The ruler declared Bahrain a kingdom in 2002 and created an elected parliament. Large protests demanding more democracy in 2011 were put down with help from neighboring countries.
funFacts: The Bahrain Fort, or Qal'at al-Bahrain, sits on a mound built up from 4,000 years of layered settlements.
Bahrain was the first Gulf Arab state to find oil, in 1932, and it built the region's first oil refinery.
The King Fahd Causeway to Saudi Arabia is about 25 kilometers long and took four years to build.
The Tree of Life has survived roughly 400 years in bare desert, and scientists still debate where it gets its water.
Bahrain's Formula 1 race in 2004 was the first Grand Prix ever held in the Middle East.
The whole country is smaller than New York City, yet it has more than 30 islands.
